feedback.problem: If $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix $A$ with characteristic polynomial $p(x)={x}^{2}-x-20,$ then ${A}^{3}=$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, let's divide the polynomial $f(x)={x}^{3}$ by characteristic polynomial $p(x)={x}^{2}-x-20,$ using long division:

|  | $\,\,x$ | $+$ | $1$ |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${x}^{2}-x-20\,$ | $\,\enclose{longdiv}{{x}^{3}\,\,}$ |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|  | ${x}^{3}$ | $-$ | ${x}^{2}$ | $-$ | $20x$ |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|  |  |  | ${x}^{2}$ | $+$ | $20x$ |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|  |  |  | ${x}^{2}$ | $-$ | $x$ | $-$ | $20$ |  |  |  |  |
|  |  |  |  |  | $21x$ | $+$ | $20$ |  |  |  |  |

Therefore, we can write ${x}^{3}$ as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3} & =q(x)p(x)+(21x+20),\end{aligned}
$$

where $q(x)=x+1.$  Replacing $x$ with $A,$ we have

$$
{A}^{3}=q(A)p(A)+(21A+20I).
$$

Now, according to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have $p(A)=O.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{3} & =q(A)p(A)+(21A+20I) \\  & =q(A)\cdot O+(21A+20I) \\  & =21A+20I.\end{aligned}
$$
